blocks.title: December 2020: from a stolen toolkit to SUNBURST

scenes.caption: Late November: FireEye investigates an alert that an employee's account had registered a second phone for two-factor codes (the device-registration alert from Logging and detection engineering).
8 December: FireEye discloses the intrusion and the tool theft, and publishes the countermeasures and CVE list on GitHub the same day.
Following every lead on how the intruders got in, FireEye reverse engineered its own SolarWinds Orion software, found the implant, and told SolarWinds on 12 December.
13 December: FireEye publishes indicators and detections for SUNBURST, the backdoor in Orion updates. The tool theft was one consequence of a much larger supply chain campaign.

blocks.md:
Kevin Mandia, FireEye's chief executive, told the US Senate Intelligence Committee in February 2021 that the company "developed more than 500 countermeasures" and had "seen no evidence to date that any attacker has used the stolen Red Team tools".

**Lessons for red teams and defenders:**

- **Red team tooling is a crown jewel.** Treat it like source code and signing keys: segmented, access-controlled, monitored.
- **Be able to detect your own red team's tools.** If your SOC cannot recognise the tools your own testers use, it cannot recognise them in an attacker's hands.
- **Most countermeasures sat low on the Pyramid of Pain.** Signatures for specific tools and files help fast, but an adversary can modify tools. The CVE list was the lasting defence: a patched system cannot be exploited through those vulnerabilities, whatever tool is used.

blocks.question: Why did FireEye publish a prioritised CVE list alongside the signatures?
options: To advertise its products
Because the CVEs were zero-days
Because patching the vulnerabilities the tools relied on defeats them whatever form the tools take
Because signatures do not work on Windows
blocks.explain: Signatures detect specific tools and can be evaded by modifying them. Removing the vulnerabilities the tools exploited closes the door regardless of tooling; FireEye stressed the tools used no zero-days.

blocks.question: What does the 'supplemental' label on a countermeasure rule tell a defender?
options: The rule is experimental and unsafe
The rule only works on FireEye products
The rule needs environment-specific tuning and suits hunting more than alerting
The rule detects zero-days
blocks.explain: FireEye's README defines supplemental rules as needing further tuning and often used in hunting workflows. Deploying them straight to alerting would flood the queue.

lessons.title: Case: cracked Cobalt Strike and the takedowns

blocks.md:
The most famous red team tool is also one of the most abused. **Cobalt Strike**, developed in 2012 and bought by Fortra in 2020, is described in its official user guide as "a platform for adversary simulations and red team operations". Its **Beacon** payload uses a "low and slow" asynchronous pattern and calls home "over DNS, HTTP, or HTTPS"; its **Malleable C2** language lets operators "reprogram Beacon to use network indicators that look like known malware or blend in with existing traffic", so that a red team can mimic a particular adversary's network traffic.

The same properties make cracked copies attractive to criminals. Infosecurity Magazine summarised the problem: threat actors "have been able to steal older versions and create cracked copies for distribution".

**The legal and police response.**

- **March 2023**: a US federal court (Eastern District of New York) [issued an order](https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2023/04/06/stopping-cybercriminals-from-abusing-security-tools/) letting Microsoft's Digital Crimes Unit, Fortra and Health-ISAC (the Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center, a non-profit for the health sector) go after "malicious infrastructure" behind cracked copies, notifying internet providers and CERTs (computer emergency response teams) so they could take servers offline. [Health-ISAC's](https://health-isac.org/microsoft-teams-up-to-take-legal-action-against-cybercriminals) chief security officer, Errol Weiss, said it would let Microsoft "take ownership of IP addresses and domains associated with command-and-control servers used by cracked copies".

- **Week of 24 June 2024: Operation Morpheus**, led by the UK National Crime Agency (NCA) with Europol (the EU's police cooperation agency) and police in several countries. It targeted "690 instances of unlicensed Cobalt Strike software hosted by 129 internet service providers in 27 countries"; by the end of the week 593 had been taken down. Private partners shared "nearly 1.2 million indicators of compromise" through MISP, the open-source Malware Information Sharing Platform.
- **March 2025**: Fortra said unauthorised copies in the wild were down 80% over two years, and that it had "seized and sinkholed over 200 malicious domains".

blocks.title: Cobalt Strike: product, abuse and disruption (years from 2012)

scenes.caption: 2012: Cobalt Strike is developed as a commercial adversary simulation tool. 2020: Fortra buys it.
March 2023: the court order lets Microsoft, Fortra and Health-ISAC have infrastructure behind cracked copies taken down through providers and CERTs.
June 2024: Operation Morpheus flags 690 servers at 129 providers in 27 countries; 593 are taken down within the week.
March 2025: Fortra reports unauthorised copies down 80% in two years. Cracked copies are reduced, not gone, and other frameworks fill the gap.

blocks.md:
**Why this matters for red and purple teams.**

- **The same tool sits on both sides.** CISA's own red team used Cobalt Strike (and Merlin, which CISA describes as a post-exploit tool that uses HTTP for C2) in AA23-059A. A Cobalt Strike detection during an exercise is therefore not evidence that it is the red team. Only deconfliction against operator logs says that (lesson 5).
- **Licensing and infrastructure are part of the ROE.** Use only licensed or open-source frameworks, restrict who can reach team servers, and destroy collected data afterwards.
- **Defenders detect the family, not the brand.** Open-source frameworks such as Sliver (from the security consultancy Bishop Fox) and Mythic, and commercial ones such as Brute Ratel C4, share the architecture of lesson 6. Detections built on behaviour (beaconing, rare destinations, injected code in memory, unusual named pipes between workstations) survive a change of framework; a detection for one product's default settings does not.

Do not write rules for a framework's defaults and call C2 covered. Malleable profiles exist precisely so that traffic can be made to look like something else, and CISA's federal red team ran more than seven different implants to prove the point (lesson 6).

blocks.question: During a red team week, the EDR flags a Cobalt Strike beacon on a finance laptop. The red team is known to use Cobalt Strike. What should happen?
options: Escalate normally; the control group deconflicts against the operator log before anyone treats it as the exercise
Close it as the red team
Uninstall the EDR
Ask the user
blocks.explain: Cracked Cobalt Strike has been used widely by criminals, so the tool name identifies nobody. Deconfliction by host, time and action is the only reliable answer.

blocks.question: Operation Morpheus flagged 690 servers and took down 593 in a week. Why is that a disruption rather than a cure?
options: Because the remaining 97 are legitimate
Because infrastructure is replaceable: it raises cost and time for criminals, but the techniques and other frameworks remain
Because Cobalt Strike was discontinued
Because court orders expire
blocks.explain: Takedowns remove servers and domains, which attackers can replace, though at a cost. Health-ISAC's chief security officer framed the aim as to 'slow them down or create distrust', not to end the problem.

lessons.title: Regulated red teaming: TIBER-EU, DORA and CBEST

blocks.md:
Financial regulators use red teaming as a supervisory tool, under the name **threat-led penetration testing** (TLPT). A bank's failure can harm the whole financial system, so regulators want evidence that defenders can detect and respond, not just a list of patched bugs.

Tiny example. A central bank tells a large payment processor: within six months, start a test in which an independent intelligence provider describes who would attack you, and an independent red team then tries to reach your payment settlement system, while your SOC is not told.

**TIBER-EU** (Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red teaming) was developed by the European Central Bank (ECB) and the EU's national central banks, published in May 2018 and "updated in 2024 to ensure its full alignment" with the TLPT rules under **DORA**, the Digital Operational Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), which requires in-scope financial entities to run TLPT at least every three years ([Article 26](https://publications.europa.eu/resource/cellar/0caf473a-85bd-11ed-9887-01aa75ed71a1.0006.03/DOC_1)). It has been adopted in over 20 countries. "The outcome is not a pass or fail": the aim is learning.

Five teams take part: the **blue team**, "whose prevention, detection and response capabilities are being tested without their foreknowledge"; the **threat intelligence provider**; the **red team testers**; the **control team**, the only people in the entity who know; and the authority's **TIBER cyber team**, which oversees the test and signs an **attestation** so other authorities can recognise it. Participants use code names for the tested entity.
**The rules that shape a TIBER-EU test**, from the 2025 framework document:

- **Scope**: the entity lists its **critical or important functions** (CIFs), the systems behind each, and at least one **flag** per system: an objective such as compromising the confidentiality, integrity or availability of that system.
- **Threat intelligence first**: a targeted report on the entity's attack surface and likely attackers, turned into scenarios.
- **At least 12 weeks of active testing**, every action logged "for the replay exercise".
- **Leg-ups**: when the red team is stuck it may be given access or information, approved by the control team and the authority, and logged. Directly providing access to flags or "disabling security controls should not be proposed as leg-ups".
- **If the blue team catches the test** or a real compromise appears, the control team proposes how to continue, or may suspend the test.
- **Closure**: red and blue reports, then a **replay** where both teams walk through the timeline together, then a **purple teaming** exercise, then a test summary, a remediation plan and the attestation.

blocks.title: TIBER-EU and CBEST phases (weeks, indicative or maximum)

scenes.caption: TIBER-EU preparation (notification, initiation, scoping, procurement) lasts at most six months, shown as 26 weeks. Threat intelligence is indicatively 4 to 6 weeks, the red team test plan 2 to 3.
Active red team testing: at least 12 weeks, so that every attack phase can be executed and the flags reached.
Closure: reports, replay and purple teaming within 10 weeks, then summary and remediation plan within 8 more; with the authority's review the whole phase can exceed 18 weeks.

CBEST, the UK scheme, for comparison: initiation about 6 weeks, threat intelligence about 10, penetration testing about 14, closure about 4. The Bank of England says projects average 9 to 12 months overall.

blocks.md: **CBEST** has been part of the UK regulators' toolkit since 2014: the Bank of England, the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) and the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). It has four phases (initiation, threat intelligence, penetration testing, closure) and a "golden thread" linking the testing to the threats against the firm's **important business services**. A **control group** of senior people "at the top of the security incident escalation chain" manages it, and the threat intelligence and penetration testing providers must be accredited (CREST, a professional body, is the accreditation and certification body). Since 2024 a complementary scheme, STAR-FS (Simulated Targeted Attack and Response for the Finance Sector), extends threat-led testing to more firms.

The 2025 CBEST thematic, drawn from 13 assessments, reads like a red team findings list: inconsistent configuration and patching, weak identity and access control including plaintext passwords, poorly tuned detection including for data exfiltration, weak segmentation, staff susceptible to social engineering, and help desks with "limited or no authentication of users".

Regulated schemes formalise everything in this course: intelligence chooses the adversary, a small control team holds the secret and the stop button, flags define success, leg-ups are logged, every action is recorded, and the test ends in a replay and purple teaming rather than a pass mark.

blocks.question: A TIBER-EU red team is stuck at the perimeter after six weeks. Which leg-up is acceptable under the framework?
options: Disabling the EDR on target servers
Giving the team direct access to the flag system
Ending the test with a pass
Giving the team a standard employee laptop and account, approved by the control team and the authority, and logged
blocks.explain: Leg-ups such as system or network access move a time-limited test forward and must be approved and logged. Handing over flags or disabling security controls is explicitly excluded, because it would stop the test measuring anything.

blocks.question: Why does TIBER-EU say the outcome is 'not a pass or fail'?
options: Because the aim is to reveal strengths and weaknesses and drive learning, which a pass mark would discourage
Because results are secret
Because tests always fail
Because regulators cannot read reports
blocks.explain: A pass/fail grade gives entities an incentive to narrow scope and hide weaknesses. Framing the test as learning, with replay, purple teaming and a remediation plan, rewards finding gaps.

lessons.title: Reporting, retesting and where to practise

blocks.md:
The engagement is not finished when the operators log off. Its value arrives as changed defences, and that requires a report people can act on, a meeting where both sides learn, and a retest that proves the fixes.

Tiny example. "We obtained Domain Admin" is a headline. "At 10:02 on day 4 we read LSASS on SRV-SP01; Sysmon event 10 was recorded but no rule fired; here is the query that would have alerted; owner: detection engineering" is a finding someone can close.

**What a red team report contains:**

- **Executive summary**: objectives, whether flags were reached, and the two or three decisions leaders need to make (see the course *Security writing and communication*).
- **Attack narrative**: a timeline of every step, from operator logs, with ATT&CK technique IDs (CISA's advisories map each step this way).
- **Detection opportunities**: for each step, which data source could have seen it and whether anything did. AA23-059A's table of expected and actual reactions is the model.
- **Findings with root causes and fixes**: not "we kerberoasted", but "service accounts with weak passwords and RC4 allowed; no rule on ticket requests".
- **Leg-ups and limits**: what was given, what was out of scope, what more time would have achieved.

**Meetings.** Vest and Tubberville describe an **executive out-brief** "within one or two days following execution", and a **technical out-brief** ("tech-on-tech"), a "bi-directional technical exchange" in which red and blue walk through the actions step by step. TIBER-EU calls the latter the replay.

nodes.label:
Fix: hardening,
log source or rule

scenes.caption: A finding starts with a step and its evidence, then a root cause and a gap type from lesson 12: visibility, logic, suppression, process or timeliness.
Every finding needs a named owner and a date. A report with 40 unowned findings changes nothing.
The fix depends on the gap: hardening (remove unconstrained delegation), a new log source (DC ticket auditing), or a rule.
Retest the same procedure. If it still fails, go back to the root cause: the diagnosis was wrong.
When it passes, the test joins the regression suite (atomics, Caldera or BAS) so the fix is proven again every month, not once.

blocks.md:
**Careers and certifications.** Red teaming usually comes after pentesting experience. Certifications aimed at it include **OSEP** from OffSec (a security training company) (OffSec Experienced Penetration Tester, from the PEN-300 course on evading defences and advanced Active Directory attacks), the certification body GIAC's **GXPN** (Exploit Researcher and Advanced Penetration Tester), and Zero-Point Security's **Red Team Ops** course, which covers adversary simulation with Cobalt Strike using a licensed copy in its labs. Purple team and detection roles value the other half of this course: emulation plans, scoring and regression testing.

**Where to practise, legally.** Only in a lab you own or on platforms that invite you:

- [Atomic Red Team](https://github.com/redcanaryco/atomic-red-team) with [Invoke-AtomicRedTeam](https://github.com/redcanaryco/invoke-atomicredteam): run tests in a lab VM with Sysmon and score your own detections.
- [Apache Caldera](https://github.com/apache/caldera): its Training plugin walks through every concept in lesson 10.
- [CTID's FIN6 intelligence summary](https://github.com/center-for-threat-informed-defense/adversary_emulation_library/blob/master/fin6/Intelligence_Summary.md) and [operations flow](https://github.com/center-for-threat-informed-defense/adversary_emulation_library/blob/master/fin6/Operations_Flow.md): see how public reporting becomes an ordered plan.
- [Blue Team Labs Online](https://blueteamlabs.online/) and [CyLab Security Academy](https://cylabacademy.org/) (a free programme from Carnegie Mellon University) for the defensive side.

Measure a red or purple team by what it changes: findings with owners, fixes retested with the same procedure, and tests that keep running afterwards. Everything is done under written authorisation, inside agreed rules, with a way to stop in minutes.

blocks.question: Which finding is most useful to a defender?
options: 'We achieved Domain Admin in four days'
'At 10:02 on day 4 we read LSASS on SRV-SP01; Sysmon 10 was logged but no rule fired; suggested rule attached; owner detection engineering'
'The network is insecure'
'We used 12 tools'
blocks.explain: It names the step, the evidence, the gap type (detection logic), a proposed fix and an owner. The others describe the red team's success, not the defenders' next action.

blocks.question: A retest of a fixed finding still fails. What should happen next?
options: Mark it fixed anyway, since work was done
Remove the test from the suite
Return to the root cause: the diagnosis or the fix was wrong
Blame the red team
blocks.explain: A failed retest means the gap is not where the team thought, for example a rule was written but the log source is not reaching the SIEM. Re-diagnosing is the point of retesting.
